Function: example or supporting detail for a claim
Main purpose: profile of a person, work or institution
Three moves: introduces a researcher, describes an aspect of the work, explains its significance
Three moves: explains a finding, generalizes it to a pattern, explains an exception
Describes how a discovery was made, then explains its importance

Describes a problem in research on a topic, then sketches a researcher’s approach to it

items.passage: Recording 20 wild greater sac-winged bat (Saccopteryx bilineata) pups, Ahana Fernandez and colleagues found that the pups’ vocal bouts, which can last as long as 43 minutes, coincide with their acquisition of the songs of adult males. Measured against the eight features that characterize human infant babbling, the pups’ vocalizations exhibited every one, including rhythmicity and the imitation of adult syllables. Babbling, the team proposes, may mark a stage of vocal learning in bats as well as in humans.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
options: It reports a finding about bat pups in order to question the idea that babbling helps young animals learn their vocalizations.
It compares the vocalizations of bat pups with human infant babbling in order to show that bat pups and human infants begin babbling at about the same age.
It reports research suggesting that a kind of vocal practice familiar from human infancy also accompanies song learning in another species.
It describes research on the vocal bouts of bat pups in order to show that pups that babble for longer periods learn adult males’ songs more quickly.
items.explanation: The text reports that sac-winged bat pups produce long, rhythmic bouts of syllables during the period in which they learn adult males’ songs, and that these bouts show all eight defining features of human infant babbling. It ends with the team’s proposal that babbling may mark a stage of vocal learning in bats as well as in humans. Choice C states this purpose: the text reports research suggesting that a behavior known from human infancy also accompanies vocal learning in another species.

A.why_wrong: The text does report a finding about bat pups, but it supports a link between babbling and learning: the bouts occur while the pups learn adult males’ songs, and the team proposes that babbling marks a stage of vocal learning.

B.why_wrong: The text does compare the pups’ vocalizations with infant babbling, but by their features, not by when babbling begins; it gives no ages for bats or for infants.

D.recipe: first clause right, word hook on “43 minutes” (LIT/INV)
D.why_wrong: The text says how long a bout can last and that the bouts coincide with song learning, but it never compares pups that babble longer with pups that babble less or says how quickly any pup learns.

sources.what: Fernandez, Knörnschild et al. 2021 (Science): 20 greater sac-winged bat pups recorded in the wild; babbling bouts up to 43 min; pup babbling shares the same eight features as human infant babbling, including imitation of canonical syllables and rhythmicity; while babbling, pups learn the song of adult males

items.notes: Area: natural science (animal behavior). Key C. Band-7 P_study modeled on 82cb7dda (a finding that a mechanism known in one group appears in another) with a different build: it opens with the fieldwork and ends on the team’s hedged proposal, not with a field of study. The source does not call the bat the only babbling mammal (it says evidence exists for very few species), so the passage claims no exclusivity. “May thus mark a stage of vocal learning” paraphrases the source’s framing (babbling marks when learning happens; parallels with vocal practice of other vocal-learning mammals). Section 6 checks: key 22 words, options 20 to 27 words (mean 23); key parts 2 (research reported; what it suggests); all three distractors keep a true first clause and fail in the second. Own blind solve before review: C. Reviewer: B and D replaced; options now 22 to 27 words.
band7_moves: hedged dual purpose: the key names the research and what it suggests
abstract key: no bat, pup or babbling wording; the student must map “vocal practice familiar from human infancy” onto babbling

all three distractors keep a true first clause (a finding about pups; a bat-human comparison; research on the pups’ bouts) and fail in the second (stance reversed; ages never given; a duration-speed link the text never draws)
architecture differs from 82cb7dda: fieldwork first, the team’s proposal last

fixes: replaced B (no infant duration given, a one-fact kill) with a first-half-true option on ages the text never gives
replaced D (mothers, killed by the stated “adult males”) with a first-half-true option linking bout length to learning speed, which the text never does

band7.why: After the fixes all three distractors keep a true first clause and fail later on content the text never supplies (stance reversed; ages; a bout-length link to learning speed); the key is a hedged, abstract two-part purpose with no bat or babbling wording, as in 82cb7dda. Before the fixes it read band 6: B and D each fell to one fact.

items.passage:
The following text is from John Galt’s 1821 novel Annals of the Parish. The narrator, a Scottish minister, records the events of 1778.

It was clear to me that the wars were not to be soon over; for I noticed, in the course of this year, that there was a greater christening of lad bairns than had ever been in any year during my incumbency; and grave and wise persons, observant of the signs of the times, said, that it had been long held as a sure prognostication of war, when the births of male children outnumbered that of females.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
options: To portray the narrator confidently judging how long a war will last from local signs that he and his neighbors trust
To show the narrator’s worry that the boys being born in the parish will one day be sent away to fight
To convey the narrator’s doubts about a prediction offered by older and more respected members of the parish
To explain how the outbreak of a war had led to an unusual increase in the number of children born and christened in the parish
items.explanation: The narrator says it was “clear” to him that the wars would not soon be over, because more boys were christened that year than in any other during his time as minister, and “grave and wise persons” held that more male than female births was a “sure prognostication of war.” The text thus portrays him confidently judging how long the war will last from a local sign that he and others in the parish trust, as choice A says.

B.why_wrong: The text does connect the boys’ births to the war, but only as a sign of how long the war will last; the narrator never worries that these boys will have to fight.

C.why_wrong: The narrator does not doubt the “grave and wise persons”: he reports their saying as support for what was already “clear” to him.

D.why_wrong: The text treats the many male births as a sign that foretells war, not as a result of the war; it gives no cause for the births at all.

sources.what: text of the excerpt (Annals of the Parish, chapter XIX, “Year 1778”); novel first published 1821

items.notes: Area: literature (novel, 1821, public domain). Excerpt copied exactly from Project Gutenberg #1310: the second paragraph of chapter XIX, “Year 1778” (the chapter title gives the year in the context line). The narrator is the Rev. Micah Balwhidder, minister of a Scottish parish, writing a yearly chronicle; the context line says only that. “Lad bairns” is left unglossed: the same sentence says “male children.” Key A. Band 6 hard (P_lit has one band-7 official, a Melville misunderstanding; this is a strong band 6): the key is a two-part paraphrase (a confident forecast; local signs the parish trusts) that shares no content word with the excerpt beyond “war”; B and D start from true details (boys born, war) and fail later; C reverses the narrator’s stance, which readers who sense Galt’s irony may misassign to the narrator: the option names the narrator’s doubts, and “It was clear to me” rules them out, so the author’s gentle irony does not make C defensible. Own blind solve before review: A.

band7.why: P_lit target 6 (its one band-7 official is an archaic misunderstanding): two-part paraphrased key; B and D start from true details (boys born, war) and D reverses sign and cause; C falls to “It was clear to me”. A fair strong band 6.

items.passage: Chinese migrants performed most of the labor on the western portion of the first transcontinental railroad, completed in 1869. <u>During one winter of construction, as many as 20,000 Chinese laborers were blasting tunnels and laying track for the Central Pacific Railroad.</u> Yet scholars with the Chinese Railroad Workers in North America Project have not recovered a single diary or letter written by any of them. Instead, the project’s researchers have reconstructed the workers’ experiences from company records, archaeological evidence, remittance contracts, and even song lyrics.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
options: It conveys the size of a workforce in order to suggest that its members were too occupied with construction to keep diaries or write letters.
It indicates how many laborers took part in construction in order to explain why the railroad was finished sooner than its builders had expected.
It provides an estimate of the number of laborers that the text goes on to question on the grounds that company records undercount them.
It establishes how large a workforce was, underscoring the text’s later point that none of its members’ own writings have been found.
items.explanation: The first sentence says Chinese migrants did most of the work on the railroad’s western portion, and the underlined sentence shows how many of them there were: as many as 20,000 at one time. The next sentence turns (“Yet”) to the fact that not a single diary or letter by any of these workers has been recovered. The size of the workforce is what makes that absence striking, so the underlined sentence establishes the scale of the workforce and underscores the later point, as choice D says.

A.recipe: first clause right, causal story invented (INV)
A.why_wrong: The sentence does convey the size of the workforce, but the text never explains why no writings have been found; the “Yet” presents their absence as surprising given so many workers, not as something the work made likely.

B.why_wrong: The sentence does indicate how many laborers took part, but the text says nothing about the railroad’s schedule; it uses the number to set up the point about missing writings.

C.why_wrong: The sentence does give an estimate, and the text later mentions company records, but as one of the sources researchers use to reconstruct the workers’ lives, not as a reason to doubt the figure.

sources.what: Chinese Railroad Workers in North America Project (Stanford): up to 20,000 Chinese blasting tunnels and laying track in one winter; about 90 percent of the western portion laid by Cantonese laborers; not one diary or letter recovered from the workers; the project drew on records, reports, archaeological findings, remittance contracts and song lyrics

items.notes: Area: history. Key D. Band-7 F_example on the 2e744883 move (a figure whose job is extent) with the clue after the span, as section 5 asks: the number matters because the next sentence says none of these workers’ writings survive. The underlined span is a full sentence, not a dash-set number as in 2e744883. “Did most of the work” stands for the source’s “90 percent of the western portion”; “company records” simplifies the source’s “records, reports.” Section 6 checks: key 23 words, options 23 to 25 words; key parts 2 (scale of the workforce; the later point it underscores); all three distractors keep a true first clause (size, number, an estimate) and fail later. Own blind solve before review: D.
band7_moves: the span is a figure of extent whose job depends on the following sentence (the “Yet” turn)
two-clause key: the scale, then the later point it underscores
all three distractors open with a true first clause and fail later (an invented reason for the missing writings; finished early; estimate questioned)
C hooks on a later detail (company records) and gives it a role the text does not give it

fixes: replaced A (letters collected, flatly contradicted by “not recovered a single diary or letter”) with a first-half-true option giving an invented reason for the missing writings

band7.why: A number of extent whose job depends on the sentence after it (the “Yet” turn), as in 2e744883; two-clause 23-word key; after replacing A all three distractors open with a true first clause and fail later (invented reason, schedule, an estimate questioned). Before the fix A fell to one stated fact.

items.passage: Begun in 1856 to measure how various fertilizers affect hay yields, the Park Grass Experiment at Rothamsted in England is the oldest ecological experiment still running. Because its plots have received largely the same treatments year after year, the experiment has gradually addressed questions its founders never anticipated. In the 1970s, researchers found that sweet vernal grass (Anthoxanthum odoratum) on neighboring plots had evolved distinct adaptations to the soil conditions that the treatments had produced, one of the first demonstrations of evolution on so small a scale.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
options: To explain how fertilizer treatments at Rothamsted raised hay yields and why English farmers adopted them
To describe a long-running field experiment and show how it has come to serve purposes beyond its original one
To argue that experiments become more valuable the longer their treatments remain unchanged
To describe a long-running field experiment and explain why its founders chose to keep each plot’s treatment the same from year to year
items.explanation: The text introduces the Park Grass Experiment, begun in 1856 to test fertilizers’ effects on hay, and notes that because its plots have been treated in largely the same way for so long, it has addressed questions its founders “never anticipated.” The example of sweet vernal grass evolving on neighboring plots shows one such new use. Choice B states this purpose: the text describes the experiment and shows how it came to serve purposes beyond its original one.

A.recipe: original purpose taken as the topic (PART/INV)
A.why_wrong: The experiment was begun to test fertilizers on hay, but the text reports no yields and says nothing about farmers; it moves at once to the questions the experiment later answered.

C.recipe: one stated reason turned into a general argument (STANCE/BROAD)
C.why_wrong: The text does link the experiment’s later uses to its long-standing treatments, but only to describe this one experiment; it makes no general argument about how experiments should be run.

D.recipe: first clause right, founders’ reason invented (INV)
D.why_wrong: The text does describe a long-running experiment, but it never gives the founders’ reasons for their design; it says only what the long-standing treatments later made possible, questions the founders “never anticipated.”

sources.what: Silvertown et al. 2006, Journal of Ecology: the Park Grass Experiment, begun in 1856, is the oldest ecological experiment in existence; its value to science has grown since it was founded to answer agricultural questions; it provided one of the first demonstrations of the evolution of adaptation at a very local scale

items.notes: Area: natural science (ecology, history of science). Key B. P_profile has no band-7 official items (band7 file, section 5), so this is a strong band 6, target 6 rather than the plan’s 7. Modeled on 3.18 (describe X and explain how it became so varied) and 3.13. The Anthoxanthum work of the 1970s (Snaydon and Davies) found local adaptation to soil conditions, including aluminium toxicity, created by the long-term treatments; the passage keeps it general (“distinct adaptations to the soil conditions”). A and D start from the experiment’s real origin and fail later; C turns the one stated reason (unchanged treatments) into a general argument. Own blind solve before review: B. Reviewer: D replaced (it now shares the key’s first clause and fails on the founders’ reasons); treatment wording softened to “largely the same.”

fixes: “each plot has received an identical treatment annually ever since” softened to “largely the same treatments year after year” (Rothamsted: liming split the plots from 1903; source abstract does not claim identical treatment)
replaced D (designed to study evolution, killed by the stated fertilizer purpose) with a first-half-true option on the founders’ reasons, which the text never gives

band7.why: P_profile has no band-7 official items, so it cannot be band 7; a strong band 6 after the fix: B and D share the first clause and D fails only on the founders’ reasons, C turns one stated reason into a general argument.

items.passage: When Julia Rohrer, Boris Egloff, and Stefan Schmukle analyzed personality data from more than 20,000 adults in Germany, the United States, and Great Britain, firstborns and later-borns proved virtually indistinguishable in extraversion, emotional stability, agreeableness, and conscientiousness; only in self-reported intellect did firstborns score slightly higher. The results sit uneasily with a long-popular belief that a child’s place among siblings shapes character in lasting ways. That belief, the data suggest, holds at most for intellectual traits, and even there the difference is slight.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
options: To present research suggesting that a widely held idea about how family position affects personality is largely mistaken
To report a study showing that birth order affects personality more strongly in Germany than in the United States or Great Britain
To explain why firstborns tend to report higher levels of intellect than their younger siblings do
To report research in order to show that birth order shapes intellectual traits as strongly as many people believe it shapes character
items.explanation: The text reports that in data from more than 20,000 adults, firstborns and later-borns were “virtually indistinguishable” in four major personality traits, with only a slight difference in self-reported intellect. It then says the results “sit uneasily” with the popular belief that birth order shapes character and that the belief holds “at most” for intellectual traits, where the difference is slight. Choice A states this purpose: the text presents research suggesting that a common idea is largely mistaken.

B.why_wrong: The study drew on adults from all three countries, but the text reports its results for the whole sample and never compares the countries.

C.recipe: one detail taken as the purpose (PART)
C.why_wrong: The text mentions that firstborns scored slightly higher in self-reported intellect but offers no explanation for it; the difference is a minor qualification, not the point of the text.

D.why_wrong: The text does report research and does find an effect only for intellectual traits, but it calls that effect slight; it never says birth order shapes intellect strongly.

sources.what: Rohrer, Egloff and Schmukle 2015 (PNAS): data from more than 20,000 adults in Germany, the USA and Great Britain; no link between birth order and extraversion, emotional stability, agreeableness or conscientiousness; small differences only in intellect (firstborns report a richer vocabulary), barely meaningful for an individual; firstborns are popularly said to be perfectionists

items.notes: Area: social science (psychology). Key A. Band 6 P_view built differently from b2’s dog-guilt item: the study comes first and the popular belief second, and the key rests on the source’s own qualification (no effect on broad traits, a slight one on intellect), so the key says “largely mistaken” and D overstates the intellect effect without using an absolute. Evaluative markers in the text: “sit uneasily,” “holds at most.” The source also found a small decline in measured intelligence from first- to last-born; the passage keeps only self-reported intellect. Own blind solve before review: A.

fixes: replaced B (later-borns higher, killed by “virtually indistinguishable”) with a first-half-true option on a country comparison the text never makes

band7.why: P_view target 6: key rests on the qualification (“largely mistaken”), D overstates the intellect effect, C takes a detail as the purpose; B now fails on an off-text country comparison instead of a stated fact.

items.passage: Tikvah Alper, a South African–born physicist, became a leading British radiobiologist through her studies of how radiation damages living cells. In the 1960s she and her colleagues turned this expertise on scrapie, a fatal brain disease of sheep, exposing infected tissue to radiation that would have inactivated a virus. The tissue remained infectious. By suggesting that the disease agent might lack nucleic acid altogether, the result helped prepare the way for the prion theory, which attributes such diseases to abnormal proteins.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
options: It introduces a researcher, describes an experiment she carried out, and then explains why later scientists rejected the experiment’s result.
It introduces a researcher, describes how she developed a treatment for a disease of animals, and then notes how widely that treatment came to be used.
It describes a disease of sheep, explains how a researcher identified its cause, and then presents the theory that she later proposed to account for the disease.
It introduces a scientist, describes how she applied her expertise to an unfamiliar problem, and then suggests why the outcome mattered for later research.
items.explanation: The first sentence introduces Tikvah Alper and her field, the study of how radiation damages cells. The next two sentences describe how she and her colleagues applied that expertise to scrapie, irradiating infected tissue that nonetheless stayed infectious. The last sentence explains the result’s importance: by suggesting the agent might lack nucleic acid, it helped prepare the way for the prion theory. Choice D gives these three moves in order.

A.why_wrong: The text does introduce Alper and describe her experiment, but it says the result helped prepare the way for a later theory, not that scientists rejected it.

B.why_wrong: Alper exposed infected tissue to radiation to learn about the disease agent; the text mentions no treatment, so there is nothing whose use could spread.

C.why_wrong: The result only suggested what the agent might lack, and the prion theory is described as a later theory her result helped prepare the way for, not one she proposed.

sources.what: Tikvah Alper: South African-born physicist and radiobiologist in Britain; with colleagues (Nature 1967) found that radiation did not kill the scrapie agent, among the first evidence that the agent does not contain nucleic acid; the finding was instrumental in the development of the prion theory, which posits a rogue protein

items.notes: Area: natural science (history of science, radiobiology). Key D. S13 has no band-7 official items, so target 6 rather than the plan’s 7. Modeled on 3.6 (introduce a researcher, describe an aspect of the work, suggest its significance). Alper herself did not accept a protein-only agent, so the passage says only that her result suggested the agent might lack nucleic acid and helped prepare the way for the prion theory; distractor C turns on exactly that difference. Paper: Alper, Cramp, Haig and Clarke, “Does the agent of scrapie replicate without nucleic acid?”, Nature 1967 (radiation work from the mid-1960s). A keeps moves 1 and 2 and breaks move 3, as most hard structure distractors do. Own blind solve before review: D.

fixes: “doses of radiation that would have destroyed any known virus” cut to “radiation that would have inactivated a virus” (the source says only that radiation did not kill the agent, evidence against a virus)

band7.why: S13 has no band-7 official items, so a strong band 6: three-move structure with A keeping moves 1 and 2 and reversing 3, C overstating her role (she did not propose the prion theory).

items.passage: Analyzing the annual growth rings of Great Basin bristlecone pines (Pinus longaeva) from three mountain ranges in California and Nevada, Matthew Salzer and colleagues found that trees within about 150 meters of the upper treeline grew more after 1950 than in any other fifty-year interval of the past 3,700 years, a surge they attribute to rising temperatures, since cold constrains growth at such elevations. Rocky Mountain bristlecone pines near their upper limit have exhibited comparable increases. Bristlecones growing farther downslope, however, displayed no such surge: there, moisture rather than cold restricts growth.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
options: It reports a finding and offers an explanation for it, notes that the finding is not unique, and then describes evidence that casts doubt on that explanation.
It reports a finding about one group of trees, notes a similar result in a related species, and then predicts that trees farther downslope will soon show the same surge.
It reports a finding and a likely cause, notes that the finding is consistent with observations elsewhere, and then accounts for trees that do not show it.
It reports a finding and offers an explanation for it, notes that other researchers have disputed that explanation, and then describes a study designed to settle the matter.
items.explanation: The first sentence reports that bristlecone pines near the upper treeline grew more after 1950 than in any fifty-year period in 3,700 years and attributes the surge to rising temperatures, since cold limits growth there. The second sentence notes a similar pattern in Rocky Mountain bristlecone pines. The third describes trees farther downslope that showed no surge and explains why: moisture, not cold, limits their growth. Choice C gives these three moves in order.

A.recipe: moves 1 and 2 right, move 3 stance flipped (STANCE)
A.why_wrong: The downslope trees do not cast doubt on the temperature explanation; the text accounts for them with the same reasoning, since their growth is limited by moisture rather than cold.

B.why_wrong: The text makes no prediction about the downslope trees; it explains that they showed no surge because moisture, not cold, limits their growth there.

D.why_wrong: No one in the text disputes the temperature explanation, and no study is designed to settle a dispute; the second sentence reports a similar finding elsewhere.

sources.what: Salzer, Hughes, Bunn and Kipfmueller 2009 (PNAS): bristlecone pines within about 150 m of upper treeline in three ranges of eastern California and Nevada grew more in the second half of the 20th century than in any 50-year period in 3,700 years; rising temperatures at high elevations are the likely cause, as cold limits growth there; at lower elevations growth is limited more by moisture; the same pattern has been seen in Rocky Mountain bristlecone pines

items.notes: Area: natural science (dendrochronology, climate). Key C. S16 has no band-7 official items (its only other official, 4ed09415, is band 6), so target 6 rather than the plan’s 7. Modeled on 3.17: finding with its cause, a pattern it fits, an exception with its cause; here all three moves rest on one limiting-factor logic. Move 2 stays within the source (Rocky Mountain bristlecones show the same high-elevation gains). Adjacent use checked: a transitions b7 item mentions bristlecone needles as a longevity comparison for Welwitschia; this item’s subject is the treeline growth study, not the tree’s age. A keeps moves 1 and 2 and flips move 3 (the 3.17 D recipe); B keeps moves 1 and 2 and invents a prediction for move 3; D breaks move 2. Own blind solve before review: C.

band7.why: S16 has no band-7 official items (its official is band 6), so a strong band 6: A keeps moves 1 and 2 and flips move 3’s stance (doubt versus consistency), which needs the limiting-factor logic to reject.

items.passage:
The following text is from Alice Hegan Rice’s 1901 novel Mrs. Wiggs of the Cabbage Patch. Mrs. Wiggs’s son Jim, who is ill, has asked her for another covering.

Mrs. Wiggs got up and went toward the bed. The three little girls lay huddled under one old quilt, their faces pale and sunken. She turned away abruptly, and looked toward the corner where Billy slept on a pallet. The blankets on his bed were insufficient even for him. She put her hands over her face, and for a moment dry sobs convulsed her. The hardest grief is often that which leaves no trace. When she went back to the stove she had a smile ready for the sick boy.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
options: To show Mrs. Wiggs deciding that her other children must give up some of their blankets for their sick brother
To portray a mother concealing her distress over her family’s poverty in order to reassure her ill son
To illustrate how Jim’s illness has spread to his younger sisters and brother
To convey Mrs. Wiggs’s relief that her other children are sleeping peacefully despite the cold
items.explanation: Looking for something more to cover Jim, Mrs. Wiggs sees that the little girls share one old quilt and that Billy’s blankets are not enough even for him. She covers her face and sobs for a moment, yet when she returns to the stove she has “a smile ready for the sick boy.” The text portrays her hiding her distress at the family’s poverty so that she can reassure her son, as choice B says.

A.why_wrong: She does look at the other children’s bedding, but it is too thin to spare; she turns away abruptly, and the text never shows her taking their blankets.

C.why_wrong: The girls’ faces are “pale and sunken” from hunger and cold, and only Jim is called “the sick boy”; nothing says his illness has spread.

D.why_wrong: The sight of the children under thin covers brings her to tears; she feels grief, not relief.

sources.what: text of the excerpt (Mrs. Wiggs of the Cabbage Patch, chapter on Jim’s illness); novel first published 1901

items.notes: Area: literature (novel, 1901, public domain). Excerpt copied exactly from Project Gutenberg #4377, one whole paragraph. Context line checked against the preceding paragraphs: it is midnight, Jim (her eldest son) is ill on a cot by the stove and asks, “Could you find a little somethin’ more to put over me, ma?” The next paragraph (left out) has her give him her own dress skirt. Key B, paraphrased away from the text (concealing distress, reassure). Length: 119 words with the attribution and context line, within the window of 2.9 and 2.19 (122 and 129), the models closest in form (a feeling conveyed through one character’s actions). Own blind solve before review: B.

items.passage: The common stork’s-bill (Erodium cicutarium) can catapult its seeds as far as half a meter from the parent plant. Each seed then depends on a long, strap-like appendage called an awn to embed it in the ground. As atmospheric humidity fluctuates, <u>the awn alternately coils and uncoils, and this repetitive twisting drives the seed into the soil like a drill</u>. Backward-facing hairs on the awn ensure that the seed advances in only one direction, so it can bury itself without any muscular effort.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined portion in the text as a whole?
options: It describes how the plant scatters its seeds away from the parent plant.
It explains why the awn is covered with backward-facing hairs.
It identifies the conditions under which the plant’s seeds begin to sprout.
It explains how the awn moves the seed into the ground.
items.explanation: The second sentence says that each seed depends on an awn to embed it in the ground. The underlined portion then explains how: as humidity changes, the awn coils and uncoils, and this repeated twisting drives the seed into the soil like a drill. Choice D describes this function.

A.why_wrong: The seeds are flung away from the plant in the first sentence; the underlined portion describes what happens after that, when the awn buries the seed.

B.why_wrong: The hairs appear in the following sentence, which says what they do; the underlined portion does not mention them.

C.why_wrong: Humidity matters here because it makes the awn coil and uncoil, not because it makes the seed sprout; germination is never discussed.

sources.what: Evangelista, Hotton and Dumais 2011 (Journal of Experimental Biology): filaree (Erodium cicutarium) launches seeds up to 0.5 m; the seed drills itself into the ground by repeatedly curling and unwinding its awn; when humidity is low the awn dries, curls and drills; backward-facing hairs make it move in one direction so it keeps drilling as it uncurls

items.notes: Area: natural science (botany, biomechanics). Key D. Modeled on 2.15 (the underlined portion explains how birds promote germination) and 2.14 (a means by which something occurs); stem and portion-length span as in 2.14 and 2.15. Common name “common stork’s-bill” (also redstem filaree). The launch is powered by the dry awns acting as springs (source); the passage says only that the plant flings its seeds. Two distractors describe the jobs of the sentences on either side of the span, the official REL/PART recipe for function items. Own blind solve before review: D.

items.passage: Common green darners (Anax junius) are among the few insects known to migrate long distances, but how individual dragonflies decide when to travel remained unclear. In a 2006 study, Martin Wikelski and colleagues <u>fitted 14 darners in coastal New Jersey with radio transmitters weighing 300 milligrams and followed their signals from airplanes and on foot</u>. The dragonflies moved only every few days, after two successive nights of falling temperatures, and remained stationary on very windy days, a pattern strikingly similar to that of migrating songbirds.
items.stem: Which choice best states the function of the underlined portion in the text as a whole?
options: To describe how researchers gathered information on the movements of individual dragonflies
To explain why green darners migrate at the same time of year as songbirds
To question the claim that insects are able to migrate long distances
To present the main finding of a study of dragonfly migration
items.explanation: The first sentence raises a problem: how individual dragonflies decide when to migrate was unclear. The underlined portion describes what the researchers did about it: they fitted darners with tiny radio transmitters and followed their signals from airplanes and on foot. The last sentence reports what they found. So the underlined portion describes how the researchers gathered their data, as choice A says.

B.why_wrong: The last sentence compares the darners’ migration pattern with that of songbirds, but neither it nor the underlined portion says the two migrate at the same time of year.

C.why_wrong: The first sentence states that green darners do migrate long distances; the underlined portion describes a method for studying that migration, not a challenge to it.

D.why_wrong: The finding, that the dragonflies moved every few days after two cold nights, is in the following sentence; the underlined portion describes the method.

sources.what: Wikelski et al. 2006 (Biology Letters), “Simple rules guide dragonfly migration”: 14 green darners fitted with 300-milligram radio transmitters, tracked from planes and on the ground in coastal New Jersey; they moved only after two successive nights of falling temperatures and stayed put on windy days, like songbirds

items.notes: Area: natural science (insect migration). Key A. Modeled on 2.20 (“To ...” options; the underlined span describes an approach a team used), with the span cut to a portion as in 2.14 and 2.15 and the 1.2 stem variant for a portion. Adjacent claim checked: a w1 boundaries item uses globe skimmer dragonflies crossing the Indian Ocean (Anderson 2009); this item is a different species, study and point (a tracking method). The fieldwork took place in 2005; the passage gives the 2006 publication. Own blind solve before review: A.

items.passage: Analyzing sediments from the Corriental reservoir, which once supplied drinking water to the Maya city of Tikal in present-day Guatemala, Kenneth Tankersley and colleagues identified zeolite and quartz sand transported from ridges about 18 miles away. Because these minerals together form a natural molecular sieve, the researchers concluded that the Maya were purifying their water over 2,000 years ago. The system is the first of its kind documented in the ancient Americas, preceding comparable European filtration by nearly two millennia.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
options: It describes how researchers made a discovery at an ancient site, then explains how the discovery led them to revise an earlier hypothesis.
It describes how researchers analyzed sediments from an ancient reservoir, then explains why their conclusions about it remain uncertain.
It explains how researchers reached a conclusion about an ancient practice, then indicates why that practice is notable.
It presents a theory about how an ancient city obtained clean water, then describes evidence that weakens that theory.
items.explanation: The first two sentences explain how Tankersley’s team reached its conclusion: they found zeolite and quartz, minerals that act as a natural sieve, in the reservoir’s sediments and concluded that the Maya used them to filter water. The last sentence says why this matters: the system is the first of its kind observed in the ancient Americas and predates similar European systems by nearly two millennia. Choice C gives these two moves in order.

A.why_wrong: The text does describe a discovery at an ancient site, but it mentions no earlier hypothesis; the last sentence explains why the filter is notable.

B.why_wrong: The researchers did analyze the reservoir’s sediments, but the text presents their conclusion with confidence and never calls it uncertain.

D.why_wrong: No theory is weakened: the text reports evidence for a conclusion, that the Maya filtered their water, and then explains its importance.

sources.what: Tankersley et al. 2020 (Scientific Reports), University of Cincinnati release: zeolite and quartz at Tikal’s Corriental reservoir formed a natural molecular sieve filtering drinking water; minerals from ridges about 18 miles away; the Maya used it more than 2,000 years ago; first observed in the ancient New World; predates similar European systems by nearly 2,000 years

items.notes: Area: history (archaeology). Key C. Modeled on 2.2 (how a discovery was made, then its importance); the importance sentence avoids 2.2’s “not only ... but also” frame. Adjacent use checked: official words_in_context 54804e10 concerns a Teotihuacán-style citadel at Tikal; this item’s subject is the reservoir filter, a different finding. Two of the three distractors keep move 1 and break move 2, the medium-tier pattern. Own blind solve before review: C.

items.passage: In 1960, a group of young Japanese architects who called themselves the Metabolists argued that buildings and cities should be able to renew themselves the way living organisms do, replacing worn-out parts while the whole lives on. Kisho Kurokawa’s Nakagin Capsule Tower, an apartment building completed in Tokyo in 1972, gave this idea a concrete form. The building’s 140 prefabricated apartments were capsules attached by high-tension bolts to two concrete towers, so that each could be detached and replaced with a new one as it aged.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
options: The text describes a disagreement among a group of architects and then explains how one building settled it.
The text presents a view of how buildings should function and then describes a building designed around that view.
The text outlines a theory of architecture and then describes a building whose design departed from that theory in important ways.
The text presents a view of how buildings should function and then explains why that view was abandoned once a building based on it was finished.
items.explanation: The first sentence presents the Metabolists’ idea that buildings and cities should renew themselves like living organisms, replacing worn-out parts. The rest of the text describes Kurokawa’s Nakagin Capsule Tower, whose capsules were bolted on so that each could be detached and replaced, a building designed to put that idea into practice. Choice B describes this structure.

A.why_wrong: The Metabolists are presented as sharing one idea, not disagreeing, and the building applies their idea rather than settling a dispute.

C.why_wrong: The tower “gave this idea a concrete form”: its replaceable capsules follow the theory rather than departing from it.

D.why_wrong: The text does present the Metabolists’ view, but it never says the view was abandoned; it ends by describing how the tower’s design reflects it.

sources.what: Nakagin Capsule Tower (Iconic Houses): a representative work of Metabolism, the idea that buildings should be renewable; designed by Kisho Kurokawa, completed in Tokyo in 1972; 140 capsule apartments on two interconnected concrete towers, connected by high-tension bolts so they could be replaced as they aged; no capsule was ever replaced

items.notes: Area: humanities and arts (architecture). Key B. Modeled on 2.10 (a philosophy, then a work influenced by it). The passage says only that each capsule could be replaced, not that any was (none ever was, and the tower was demolished in 2022), so it does not imply replacement. The Metabolist manifesto was presented in 1960 at the World Design Conference in Tokyo. A is a wholly wrong template; C and D keep the first move’s subject and fail in the second. Own blind solve before review: B.

items.passage: For most of the history of the transatlantic slave trade, captives’ names went unrecorded once they were forced aboard ship, making it difficult to know where in Africa they had come from. After Britain outlawed the trade in 1807, however, courts in Freetown, Sierra Leone, and Havana, Cuba, registered the names of Africans freed from intercepted ships. Historian David Eltis and his colleagues have put these names online, asking people who recognize a name to identify the language and culture it belongs to, and so its bearer’s likely homeland.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
options: It points out a limitation of early slave-trade records, then explains that courts were created in the 1800s specifically to correct it.
It describes how courts in two cities recorded the names of freed Africans, then explains why those records were long kept secret.
It explains why the origins of many enslaved Africans are hard to trace, then argues that historians should stop relying on names to trace them.
It identifies a difficulty in learning about certain people’s origins, then describes a project designed to overcome it.
items.explanation: The first sentence states the problem: captives’ names went unrecorded once they were forced aboard ship, so it is hard to know where in Africa they came from. The rest of the text describes Eltis’s approach: using names registered by courts after 1807 and asking people who recognize a name to identify its language and culture, and so its bearer’s likely homeland. Choice D gives these two moves.

A.why_wrong: The courts did register names, but they handled Africans freed from intercepted ships after the trade was outlawed; nothing says they were created to fix gaps in the records.

B.why_wrong: The courts’ registers are one part of the text, not its opening problem, and nothing suggests they were kept secret; Eltis’s team has put the names online.

C.why_wrong: The text does explain why origins are hard to trace, but the names are the solution it describes, not something historians should abandon.

sources.what: African Origins project (Emory): for most of the slave trade, captives’ names were lost once they were forced aboard; after the trade was outlawed in 1807, courts intercepting slave ships recorded their names; visitors who recognize a name identify the modern country, language and culture that use it; David Eltis leads the project

items.notes: Area: history. Key D. Modeled on 2.16 (a problem in research on a topic, then a researcher’s approach); the key avoids 2.16’s wording and its distractors avoid the “avoid those sources altogether” recipe. Courts of Mixed Commission sat in Freetown and Havana (Emory Report 2010); the 2012 source counts more than 90,000 surviving register entries, so the passage says only that the courts registered names. A and C keep move 1 and break move 2. Own blind solve before review: D.

items.passage:
The following text is adapted from Henry Lawson’s 1897 poem “The Uncultured Rhymer to His Cultured Critics.”

You were quick to pick on a faulty line
That I strove to put my soul in:
Your eyes were keen for a ‘dash’ of mine
In the place of a semi-colon—
And blind to the rest. And is it for such
As you I must brook restriction?
‘I was taught too little?’ I learnt too much
To care for a pedant’s diction!

Must I turn aside from my destined way
For a task your Joss [idol] would find me?
items.stem: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
options: The speaker responds to critics who fault his writing, then insists that he will keep to his own chosen path.
The speaker admits that his lack of schooling has weakened his poems, then asks his critics to help him improve them.
The speaker praises his critics for their careful reading, then explains why he has decided to accept their advice.
The speaker recalls a disagreement about punctuation, then predicts that his critics will soon change their opinion of his work.
items.explanation: In the first stanza the speaker answers critics who seized on “a faulty line” and a dash used in place of a semicolon while staying “blind to the rest,” and he turns their charge that he was “taught too little” back on them. In the last lines he asks whether he must “turn aside from my destined way” for a task they would set him, a question that insists he will not. The poem responds to criticism of his writing and then affirms his commitment to his own course, as choice A says.

B.why_wrong: “I was taught too little?” repeats the critics’ charge as a question, and he answers that he “learnt too much / To care for a pedant’s diction”; he concedes nothing and asks for no help.

C.why_wrong: Their eyes were “keen” only for small faults and “blind to the rest”; this is a complaint, and he refuses their advice rather than accepting it.

D.why_wrong: The dash and semicolon are one example of the critics’ fault-finding, and the speaker makes no prediction about their opinions; he says he will not turn aside from his own way.

sources.what: text of the excerpt (Verses Popular and Humorous, 1900, pp. 111–112); the poem first appeared in The Bulletin, 25 December 1897, per AustLit and the Coolabah article on Lawson and John Le Gay Brereton
Barnes, “An uncultured rhymer and his cultured critics” (Coolabah 2014): the poem dated 1897, written to John Le Gay Brereton after his comment on Lawson’s prosody

items.notes: Area: literature (poem, 1897, public domain). Excerpt copied exactly from Project Gutenberg #52066: the fourth stanza and the first two lines of the fifth, ending at a full stop (“find me?”); Gutenberg’s “--” rendered as a closed em dash; “Joss” glossed “[idol]”, hence “adapted.” The poem answered Brereton, a university-educated friend who had criticized Lawson’s prosody; no context line, since the title names the critics and a line about the quarrel would hand over move 1. The ambition move is a commitment (“Must I turn aside from my destined way”), so the key says “keep to his own chosen path,” not a grand ambition. Length 97 words with the attribution (2.21: 100). Own blind solve before review: A.

fixes: added a source for the 1897 date (Barnes, Coolabah 2014; AustLit lists The Bulletin, 25 December 1897)

items.passage: Why is the skin of the African elephant (Loxodonta africana) crisscrossed by an intricate network of minuscule channels? Using microscopy and computer simulations, Michel Milinkovitch and colleagues determined that the channels are fractures in the skin’s brittle outer layer, which elephants do not shed in the usual way. As that layer progressively thickens over the tiny elevations covering the skin, bending stress accumulates in the valleys between them until the layer cracks. The researchers suggest that these fractures benefit the animals: the channels retain water, which helps elephants stay cool, and help mud adhere to the skin, protecting it from intense sunlight and parasites.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
options: The text raises a question about elephants, then explains why researchers have so far been unable to answer it.
The text describes a common belief about elephants, then presents evidence showing that the belief is mistaken.
The text poses a question about a physical feature of an animal, then presents a research team’s explanation for it.
The text asks why an animal’s skin looks the way it does, then compares that skin with the skin of other large mammals.
items.explanation: The text opens with a question: why is the African elephant’s skin crisscrossed by tiny channels? The rest presents Milinkovitch’s team’s answer: the channels are cracks in the brittle outer layer, formed as it thickens and bends over the skin’s bumps, and they help the animals by holding water and mud. Choice C describes this structure.

A.why_wrong: The question is answered: the researchers explain how the channels form and how they may help elephants.

B.why_wrong: The text begins with a question, not a belief, and nothing in it is shown to be mistaken.

D.why_wrong: The text says elephants do not shed the outer layer “in the usual way,” but it never compares their skin with that of any other large mammal.

sources.what: Martins, Milinkovitch et al. 2018 (Nature Communications), University of Geneva release: the minuscule crevices on African elephant skin are true fractures of the brittle, shedding-deficient outer layer, caused by bending stress in the valleys between millimetric elevations; they retain 5 to 10 times more water than flat skin; mud protects against parasites

items.notes: Area: natural science (biology, biomechanics). Key C. Modeled on 2.24 (a question, then a possible answer). The source names António Martins as first author and Michel Milinkovitch as leader; the passage names Milinkovitch “and colleagues.” Sun protection is in the paper’s abstract (protection against parasites and intense solar radiation by mud adherence). Options vary their openings so that no three share one long prefix; A and D keep move 1 and break move 2. Own blind solve before review: C.

items.passage:
The following text is from Fanny Fern’s 1854 novel Ruth Hall. Ruth and her husband are spending the summer at a resort hotel called Beach Cliff.

<u>Hotel life is about the same in every latitude.</u> At Beach Cliff there was the usual number of vapid, fashionable mothers; dressy, brainless daughters; half-fledged wine-bibbing sons; impudent, whisker-dyed roués; bachelors, anxious to give their bashfulness an airing; bronchial clergymen, in search of health and a text; waning virgins, languishing by candle-light; gouty uncles, dyspeptic aunts, whist-playing old ladies, flirting nursery maids and neglected children.
items.stem: Which choice best states the function of the underlined sentence in the overall structure of the text?
options: It introduces a setting that the following sentence goes on to describe in terms of its natural surroundings.
It offers a generalization that the following sentence illustrates with the guests at one hotel.
It establishes a contrast with the description of the hotel’s guests in the following sentence.
It summarizes the narrator’s praise for Beach Cliff, which the following sentence elaborates on.
items.explanation: The underlined sentence makes a general claim: hotel life is the same everywhere. The next sentence bears it out with a list of the “usual” guests at Beach Cliff, from fashionable mothers and brainless daughters to gouty uncles and neglected children. So the underlined sentence offers a generalization that the following sentence illustrates, as choice B says.

A.why_wrong: The following sentence does describe Beach Cliff, but through the people staying there, not through any natural surroundings.

C.why_wrong: The list of “the usual number” of familiar types confirms that hotel life is the same everywhere; it does not contrast with the underlined claim.

D.why_wrong: The guests are described mockingly (“vapid,” “brainless,” “whisker-dyed”); neither sentence praises Beach Cliff.

sources.what: text of the excerpt (Ruth Hall, chapter XXV); novel first published 1854

items.notes: Area: literature (novel, 1854, public domain). Excerpt copied exactly from Project Gutenberg #40814: the opening paragraph of chapter XXV. Context checked: Beach Cliff is the hotel where Ruth and her husband Harry spend the summer (the chapter goes on to Ruth’s friendship with another guest; later chapters say Harry met friends there “during the pleasant summer”); the following paragraph mentions sails upon a lake, so the context line says “resort hotel,” not seaside. Key B. Modeled on 2.13 (stem copied; the span sets up the description that follows), with a generalization instead of a character sketch so the frame differs. Own blind solve before review: B.

items.passage:
The following text is from Carroll Watson Rankin’s 1904 novel Dandelion Cottage.

The little one-story cottage, too much out of repair to be rented, stood empty and neglected. To most persons it was an unattractive spot if not actually an eyesore. The steps sagged in a dispirited way, some of the windows were broken, and <u>the fence, in sympathy perhaps with the house, had shed its pickets and leaned inward with a discouraged, hopeless air</u>.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined portion in the text as a whole?
options: It reinforces the impression that the cottage is rundown and forlorn.
It suggests that the fence was damaged by people who disliked the cottage.
It indicates that the neighbors feel sorry for the empty cottage.
It shows that the cottage is about to be repaired so that it can be rented.
items.explanation: The text describes the cottage as empty, neglected, and an eyesore, with sagging steps and broken windows. The underlined portion adds the fence, which has lost its pickets and leans inward with a “discouraged, hopeless air,” as though it shared the house’s gloom. It reinforces the impression that the cottage is rundown and forlorn, as choice A says.

B.why_wrong: The fence has “shed its pickets” through neglect; nothing says anyone damaged it.

C.why_wrong: The “sympathy” belongs to the fence, imagined as sharing the house’s mood; no neighbors are described.

D.why_wrong: The cottage is “too much out of repair to be rented,” and nothing says repairs are coming.

sources.what: text of the excerpt (Dandelion Cottage, chapter I); novel first published 1904

items.notes: Area: literature (novel, 1904, public domain). Excerpt copied exactly from Project Gutenberg #37871, one whole paragraph (the cottage the four girls later turn into a playhouse). No context line is needed: the paragraph introduces the cottage itself. Key A. Modeled on 1.1 (an image of a place that conveys a feeling) and 1.20. Own blind solve before review: A.

items.passage:
The following text is from George Madden Martin’s 1902 novel Emmy Lou: Her Book and Heart. Emmy Lou, a schoolgirl, has been seated away from her friend Hattie by their teacher.

And so Emmy Lou and Hattie were separated. But there were three new little girls near Emmy Lou. Their kid button-shoes had tassels. Very few little girls had button-shoes. Button-shoes were new. Emmy Lou had button-shoes. She was proud of them. <u>But they did not have tassels.</u>
items.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
options: It indicates that Emmy Lou plans to ask her family for shoes like the new girls’ shoes.
It shows that the new girls have been teasing Emmy Lou about her shoes.
It explains why Emmy Lou is unhappy about being separated from Hattie.
It suggests that Emmy Lou now feels less proud of her own shoes.
items.explanation: Emmy Lou is proud of her button-shoes, which few girls have. But the new girls’ button-shoes have tassels, and the underlined sentence notes that hers “did not have tassels.” Coming right after “She was proud of them,” the sentence suggests that her pride has been dimmed by the comparison, as choice D says.

A.why_wrong: The text says nothing about Emmy Lou asking for new shoes; it only notes what her shoes lack.

B.why_wrong: The new girls are only described as sitting near Emmy Lou with tasseled shoes; nothing says they mention her shoes at all.

C.why_wrong: The separation from Hattie is mentioned in the first sentence, but the underlined sentence is about the shoes, not about Hattie.

sources.what: text of the excerpt (Emmy Lou: Her Book and Heart, chapter on the Fourth Reader); novel first published 1902

items.notes: Area: literature (novel, 1902, public domain). Excerpt copied exactly from Project Gutenberg #24347, one whole paragraph. Context checked: on the first day the teacher, Miss Lizzie, asked which desk-mates the girls preferred and then seated all such pairs apart, so Emmy Lou and Hattie were separated; the context line says only that. Key D. Modeled on 1.21 (the underlined portion indicates a feeling) and 1.1. Own blind solve before review: D.

items.passage: Clementine Hunter spent most of her life on Melrose Plantation in Louisiana, where she picked cotton and later worked as a cook and laundress. Although she did not begin painting until approximately age fifty, she produced more than five thousand works, many depicting the agricultural labor, religious ceremonies, and social gatherings of the Black community along the Cane River. In 1955, Hunter became the first African American artist granted a solo exhibition at New Orleans’s Delgado Museum, a remarkable recognition for a painter who had begun so late.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
options: To argue that museums should collect more work by artists who began painting late in life
To explain how Hunter’s painting style changed after her 1955 exhibition
To give an overview of Hunter’s life and work and an important recognition she received
To compare Hunter’s paintings of Cane River life with those of other Louisiana artists
items.explanation: The text describes Hunter’s working life on Melrose Plantation, her start as a painter at about fifty, the thousands of works she produced and their subjects, and her 1955 solo exhibition at the Delgado Museum, the first there for an African American artist. Choice C states this purpose.

A.why_wrong: The text describes one artist’s life and work; it makes no recommendation to museums.

B.why_wrong: The 1955 exhibition is the last thing the text mentions; it says nothing about her style before or after it.

D.why_wrong: No other Louisiana artists are mentioned.

sources.what: Clementine Hunter (64 Parishes, Louisiana Endowment for the Humanities): picked cotton at Melrose Plantation, later a cook and laundress; did not begin painting until age fifty; more than five thousand works, often depicting the lives of African Americans in the Cane River community; in 1955 the first African American artist to have a solo exhibition at the Delgado Museum

items.notes: Area: humanities and arts (painting). Key C. Modeled on 1.4 (examples of a composer’s importance) and 1.6 (overview of history and importance). The often-told story that she began with paints left by a visiting artist, and the label “self-taught,” are not in the source and are left out (the source says Melrose’s resident artists inspired her). The Delgado Museum is now the New Orleans Museum of Art. Own blind solve before review: C.

items.passage:
The following text is from Mary Grant Bruce’s 1910 novel A Little Bush Maid. Norah, a twelve-year-old girl, lives on a cattle station [ranch] in Australia.

Norah turned from the creek and entered the scrub. She loved the bush, and was never happier than when exploring its recesses. A born bushmaid, she had never any difficulty about finding her way in the scrub, or of retracing her steps. The faculty of bushmanship must be born in you; if you have it not naturally, training very rarely gives it.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
options: To explain how Norah learned to find her way through the bush
To convey Norah’s delight in the bush and her natural skill at moving through it
To describe Norah’s fear of getting lost in an unfamiliar place
To show that Norah would rather explore alone than spend time with her family
items.explanation: Norah “loved the bush” and was “never happier” than when exploring it, and as “a born bushmaid” she never had trouble finding her way or retracing her steps. The text conveys her delight in the bush and her natural skill there, as choice B says.

A.why_wrong: The text says her skill is inborn and that “training very rarely gives it”; it does not describe her learning it.

C.why_wrong: She never had “any difficulty” finding her way and is happiest exploring; she shows no fear.

D.why_wrong: The text says exploring the bush makes her happiest, but it never compares this with time spent with her family.

sources.what: text of the excerpt (A Little Bush Maid, chapter on the camping trip); novel first published 1910

items.notes: Area: literature (novel, 1910, public domain). Excerpt copied exactly from Project Gutenberg #8730, one whole paragraph; “station [ranch]” is a gloss in the context line only. Context checked: Norah Linton, twelve, lives on Billabong, a cattle station in Victoria; in this chapter she leaves the creek where the others are fishing to go for a walk. The source’s preceding dialogue is left out. Key B, paraphrased (delight, natural skill). Own blind solve before review: B.

items.passage:
The following text is from Ralph Connor’s 1902 novel Glengarry School Days.

Ranald always hated new clothes. He felt them an intolerable burden. He did not mind his new homespun, home-made flannel check shirt of mixed red and white, but the heavy fulled-cloth suit made by his Aunt Kirsty felt like a suit of mail. He moved heavily in it and felt queer, and knew that he looked as he felt. The result was that he was in no genial mood, and was on the alert for any indication of levity at his expense.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
options: To explain why Ranald’s aunt made him a heavy suit for the coming winter
To describe the materials and colors of Ranald’s new shirt and suit
To show that Ranald is proud of the clothes his aunt made for him
To portray Ranald’s discomfort in his new clothes and his readiness to take offense
items.explanation: Ranald “always hated new clothes”: his heavy suit feels “like a suit of mail,” he moves heavily and feels “queer,” and as a result he is “on the alert for any indication of levity at his expense,” ready to resent any joke about how he looks. The text portrays his discomfort and his touchiness, as choice D says.

A.why_wrong: The text says his aunt made the suit but gives no reason for it and never mentions winter.

B.why_wrong: The text names the shirt’s check pattern and the suit’s cloth, but only on the way to showing how Ranald feels in them.

C.why_wrong: He “hated new clothes” and felt them “an intolerable burden”; he is not proud of them.

sources.what: text of the excerpt (Glengarry School Days, chapter on the examination day); novel first published 1902

items.notes: Area: literature (novel, 1902, public domain). Excerpt copied exactly from Project Gutenberg #3243, one whole paragraph. No context line: the paragraph is self-contained, and a line about the school examination day (the occasion for the new clothes) would add nothing the question needs. Key D. Own blind solve before review: D.

items.passage: Some musicians and scientists have converted climate measurements into music, hoping that listeners will grasp through sound what conventional graphs struggle to communicate. <u>In 2013, Daniel Crawford, then a student at the University of Minnesota, composed a piece for cello in which each note represents one year from 1880 to 2012, with higher pitches corresponding to warmer global temperatures.</u> Performed in sequence, the notes gradually ascend as the planet warms.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
options: It provides an example of the practice described in the first sentence.
It explains why graphs are a poor way to present scientific data.
It describes how Crawford first became interested in climate science.
It presents a criticism of using music to communicate scientific information.
items.explanation: The first sentence says that some people have converted climate measurements into music. The underlined sentence describes one case: Crawford’s cello piece, in which each note stands for a year and higher notes mean warmer years. It provides an example of the practice the first sentence describes, as choice A says.

B.why_wrong: The first sentence mentions what conventional graphs struggle to communicate; the underlined sentence describes a piece of music and says nothing about graphs.

C.why_wrong: The text says only that Crawford was a student when he wrote the piece, not how his interest began.

D.why_wrong: The text presents turning data into music as a way to help listeners grasp it; nothing in the underlined sentence criticizes it.

sources.what: “A Song of Our Warming Planet” (2013): University of Minnesota student Daniel Crawford’s cello piece from NASA GISS surface temperature data, one note per year from 1880 to 2012, low notes for cool years and high notes for warm ones; meant as a tool for people who connect with music more than graphs

items.notes: Area: humanities and arts (music, with climate science). Key A. Modeled on 1.3 (the underlined sentence gives one example of what the previous sentences describe) and 1.14. The source does not name Crawford’s field, so the passage calls him a student only. Own blind solve before review: A.

items.passage: Although most novels have a single author, a few have been produced collaboratively, with each contributor responsible for writing one chapter. In The Whole Family (1908), twelve authors, among them William Dean Howells and Henry James, each narrated a portion of one family’s story from the perspective of a different relative. In The Floating Admiral (1931), members of a London association of detective novelists, including Agatha Christie and Dorothy L. Sayers, took turns composing successive chapters of a single murder mystery.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
options: The text explains why most novels have a single author, then argues that novels written by groups are better.
The text compares the careers of two famous authors, then explains how their working methods differed.
The text describes an unusual way of writing novels, then illustrates it with two specific cases.
The text describes a dispute among a group of writers, then explains how the dispute was resolved.
items.explanation: The first sentence describes a general situation: although most novels have one author, a few were written by many, each contributing a chapter. The next two sentences give two examples, The Whole Family (1908) and The Floating Admiral (1931). Choice C describes this structure.

A.why_wrong: The text notes that most novels have one author but gives no reason for it and makes no claim that group novels are better.

B.why_wrong: The text names several authors as contributors to two books; it does not compare any two authors’ careers.

D.why_wrong: The writers in each example worked together on one book; no dispute is described.

sources.what: The Whole Family: A Novel by Twelve Authors (1908): a collaborative novel in twelve chapters, each by a different author and each told by a different family member, conceived by William Dean Howells; Henry James wrote one chapter

items.notes: Area: humanities (literary history). Key C. Modeled on 1.12 (a general situation, then specific examples). The second example, The Floating Admiral (1931), was written chapter by chapter by members of the Detection Club, including Agatha Christie and Dorothy L. Sayers (well known; the one source covers the core claim and the first example). Own blind solve before review: C.

items.passage: Conservation laws usually protect two kinds of living things: plants and animals. Fungi, which make up a separate biological kingdom, typically receive no mention, even though they decompose organic material into soil and help many plants absorb water and nutrients. Protecting habitats while ignoring the fungi that sustain them leaves conservation incomplete. Largely through the advocacy of mycologist Giuliana Furci, Chile became the first country to protect fungi by law. Other nations should follow its example.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
options: To explain how fungi help plants absorb water and nutrients
To argue that fungi deserve a place in efforts to protect living things
To describe how Chile’s environmental laws have changed over the past century
To question whether fungi should be considered a separate kingdom of life
items.explanation: The text says conservation laws usually protect only plants and animals and leave out fungi, although fungi do important work, and it calls conservation that ignores them “incomplete.” It points to Chile as the first country to protect fungi by law and ends, “Other nations should follow its example.” The text argues that fungi should be included in conservation, as choice B says.

A.recipe: supporting detail taken as the purpose (PART)
A.why_wrong: The text mentions that fungi help plants absorb water and nutrients only as a reason fungi deserve protection; it does not explain how they do it.

C.why_wrong: Chile is mentioned once, as an example for other nations; the text gives no history of its laws.

D.why_wrong: The text states that fungi make up a kingdom of their own; it does not question it.

sources.what: Undark 2021, “Flora, Fauna, and Funga”: environmental laws still think of biodiversity as flora and fauna, which excludes fungi; Giuliana Furci and allied nonprofits proposed in 2010 that Chile assess developments’ effects on fungi, and Chile became the first country in the world to protect fungi by law; fungi help plants get water and nutrients and break down organic matter into soil

items.notes: Area: natural science (conservation policy). Key B, paraphrased (“deserve a place in efforts to protect”). Modeled on 1.22 (an argument with an explicit evaluative close). The year of Chile’s law is left out (sources give 2012 to 2014). Own blind solve before review: B.

items.passage: Analyzing residues on ceramic vessels from Santa Ana-La Florida, an ancient settlement in the upper Amazon region of Ecuador, Sonia Zarrillo and colleagues determined that inhabitants were consuming cacao, the source of chocolate, approximately 5,300 years ago. The team identified the cacao through starch granules, ancient DNA, and theobromine, a compound found in the cacao tree but not in its wild relatives. <u>The earliest known evidence of cacao consumption had previously come from Central America</u>, but the Ecuadorian residues predate any discovered there by roughly 1,500 years.
items.stem: Which choice best states the function of the underlined portion in the text as a whole?
options: It explains how the researchers identified cacao residues on the vessels.
It presents a claim that the rest of the sentence goes on to support with additional evidence.
It describes the main goal of the study introduced in the first sentence.
It gives background that helps show why the comparison in the rest of the sentence matters.
items.explanation: The underlined portion says that the oldest known evidence of cacao use had come from Central America. The rest of the sentence says the Ecuador residues are about 1,500 years older than any found there. Knowing where the earlier evidence came from shows why the new finding is significant, so the underlined portion gives background for the comparison that follows, as choice D says.

A.why_wrong: The previous sentence says how the team identified the cacao (starch granules, ancient DNA, theobromine); the underlined portion concerns earlier evidence from elsewhere.

B.why_wrong: The rest of the sentence does not support the underlined claim; it shows that the claim no longer holds, since the Ecuador residues are older.

C.why_wrong: The underlined portion reports what earlier evidence showed, not what the researchers set out to do.

sources.what: Zarrillo et al. 2018 (Nature Ecology & Evolution), Science News: pottery from Santa Ana-La Florida in Ecuador’s upper Amazon shows cacao use about 5,300 years ago, based on starch grains, theobromine residues (a compound in the cacao tree but not its wild relatives) and ancient cacao DNA, about 1,500 years before cacao use in Central America

items.notes: Area: history (archaeology). Key D, worded away from 1.2’s key (“provides context that clarifies the significance”). Modeled on 1.2 (a previous belief set against a new find in one sentence). Adjacent claim checked: a w1 boundaries item uses cacao residues in Pueblo Bonito jars (Crown and Hurst 2009); this item is a different site, region and finding. Own blind solve before review: D.
